stimulus.title: Social Science: Keeping a Language Alive
stimulus.text:
When linguists speak of a language as endangered, they rarely mean that its words are disappearing from dictionaries. Dictionaries, after all, can preserve a language indefinitely, in the way a museum preserves a fossil. What linguists mean is that fewer and fewer children are learning it at home. A language can have tens of thousands of speakers and still be in danger if almost all of those speakers are grandparents; it can have only a few hundred and be relatively secure if those few hundred include toddlers. The crucial measure is not size but transmission: whether the language is being handed from one generation to the next.

Transmission tends to break down for reasons that have little to do with the language itself. When a family moves to a city, when schools teach in a single national language, when jobs and opportunity seem to require a different tongue, parents often make a reasonable calculation: their children will be better served by the language of power. Sometimes the calculation is forced on them. In many countries, children were punished in school for speaking their home language well into the twentieth century, and the shame attached to that punishment could last long after the policy ended.

Efforts to reverse this process, known as language revitalization, have multiplied in recent decades, and they have taught advocates some uncomfortable lessons. The first is that documentation, however valuable, is not the same as revival. Recording elderly speakers, compiling grammars, and archiving stories can preserve an extraordinary amount of knowledge, and these materials are often indispensable to later learners. But a language that exists only in recordings is, in an important sense, no longer being used to do anything: to argue, to joke, to comfort a child at night.

The second lesson is that classroom instruction alone rarely produces fluent speakers. A child who studies a heritage language for an hour a day, then spends the rest of the day in the dominant language, may learn a great deal about it without ever coming to think in it. For this reason, some of the most closely watched programs are immersion programs, in which young children spend the entire school day, and sometimes much of their home life, in the language being revived. The approach demands enormous resources: teachers who are fluent, materials that must often be written from scratch, and families willing to commit to it.

A third lesson concerns what counts as success. Revitalized languages almost always change. New learners, many of whom grew up speaking another language first, bring with them sounds, idioms, and patterns of grammar from that language. Elders sometimes find the speech of younger speakers jarring, even incorrect. Linguists who study these situations tend to be less troubled. Every living language changes, they point out, and a language spoken imperfectly by children is in a far stronger position than one spoken perfectly by no one.

This view is not universally shared, and the disagreement is not merely academic. For some communities, the purpose of revitalization is to recover a connection with ancestors, and a language that has drifted far from the speech of those ancestors may feel like a loss disguised as a gain. For others, the purpose is to give the language a future, and change is the price of that future. Both positions reflect real values, and the programs that seem to last are often those that make room for both, treating elders as the keepers of an authoritative tradition while allowing young speakers to make the language their own.

What revitalization cannot do is simply restore the past. A language that returns from the edge of disappearance returns into a different world from the one it left. That may be the most important lesson of all: a revived language is not a relic brought back to life but a new chapter in an old story, written by people who decided the story was worth continuing.

stimulus.title: Social Science: Keeping a Language Alive
stimulus.text:
When linguists speak of a language as endangered, they rarely mean that its words are disappearing from dictionaries. Dictionaries, after all, can preserve a language indefinitely, in the way a museum preserves a fossil. What linguists mean is that fewer and fewer children are learning it at home. A language can have tens of thousands of speakers and still be in danger if almost all of those speakers are grandparents; it can have only a few hundred and be relatively secure if those few hundred include toddlers. The crucial measure is not size but transmission: whether the language is being handed from one generation to the next.

Transmission tends to break down for reasons that have little to do with the language itself. When a family moves to a city, when schools teach in a single national language, when jobs and opportunity seem to require a different tongue, parents often make a reasonable calculation: their children will be better served by the language of power. Sometimes the calculation is forced on them. In many countries, children were punished in school for speaking their home language well into the twentieth century, and the shame attached to that punishment could last long after the policy ended.

Efforts to reverse this process, known as language revitalization, have multiplied in recent decades, and they have taught advocates some uncomfortable lessons. The first is that documentation, however valuable, is not the same as revival. Recording elderly speakers, compiling grammars, and archiving stories can preserve an extraordinary amount of knowledge, and these materials are often indispensable to later learners. But a language that exists only in recordings is, in an important sense, no longer being used to do anything: to argue, to joke, to comfort a child at night.

The second lesson is that classroom instruction alone rarely produces fluent speakers. A child who studies a heritage language for an hour a day, then spends the rest of the day in the dominant language, may learn a great deal about it without ever coming to think in it. For this reason, some of the most closely watched programs are immersion programs, in which young children spend the entire school day, and sometimes much of their home life, in the language being revived. The approach demands enormous resources: teachers who are fluent, materials that must often be written from scratch, and families willing to commit to it.

A third lesson concerns what counts as success. Revitalized languages almost always change. New learners, many of whom grew up speaking another language first, bring with them sounds, idioms, and patterns of grammar from that language. Elders sometimes find the speech of younger speakers jarring, even incorrect. Linguists who study these situations tend to be less troubled. Every living language changes, they point out, and a language spoken imperfectly by children is in a far stronger position than one spoken perfectly by no one.

This view is not universally shared, and the disagreement is not merely academic. For some communities, the purpose of revitalization is to recover a connection with ancestors, and a language that has drifted far from the speech of those ancestors may feel like a loss disguised as a gain. For others, the purpose is to give the language a future, and change is the price of that future. Both positions reflect real values, and the programs that seem to last are often those that make room for both, treating elders as the keepers of an authoritative tradition while allowing young speakers to make the language their own.

What revitalization cannot do is simply restore the past. A language that returns from the edge of disappearance returns into a different world from the one it left. That may be the most important lesson of all: a revived language is not a relic brought back to life but a new chapter in an old story, written by people who decided the story was worth continuing.
